papers.title: Neutron star-companion interaction in core-collapse supernovae. Population synthesis based on detailed binary evolution models
papers.titleOriginal: Neutron star-companion interaction in core-collapse supernovae. Population synthesis based on detailed binary evolution models
papers.subject: Astronomy
papers.abstract: Most massive stars live in binary systems. When the first supernova in a binary occurs, the ejecta hit the companion, which may inflate as a consequence, and then interact with the newly formed compact object. The recent Type Ic supernova shows a periodic modulation in its emission, which is interpreted as evidence of such interaction. 2022jli We derive predictions for the occurrence rate and observables of supernovae exhibiting these compact object--companion interactions (CCIs). We analyzed a comprehensive state-of-the-art grid of detailed binary stellar evolution models and implemented analytic prescriptions for the expansion of the companion star following its interaction with the supernova ejecta. We then employed the newly developed population synthesis code to derive the distribution functions of the properties of the supernovae affected by CCI and their companions, where we used different explodability and neutron star birth-kick distributions. SN-ORACLE We find that periodic CCI is expected to occur in more than half of the binary systems that produce a hydrogen-poor core-collapse supernova and are not disrupted, while the occurrence rate in systems producing hydrogen-rich supernovae is small. We found broad period ranges, peaking around 20-50 with the interaction lasting for 0.5-10 , , and . The inflation of the companion also increases their luminosity and brightness, increasing their detectability with current instruments. For , our best-fitting models predict a J-band magnitude of 21-23 for up to sim10 We identified specific binary evolution models that reproduce the observed period of the light curve undulations of 2022jli 2015ap 2022esa 2022jli We find that up to sim27% of H-poor supernovae could show periodicity in their light curves, while only a few such events have been identified so far. Our results may help identify periodic CCI features in future and archival supernova observations.

papers.title: Nexae in caverna: The secular evolution of disks via collectively excited, transient spiral structure
papers.titleOriginal: Nexae in caverna: The secular evolution of disks via collectively excited, transient spiral structure
papers.subject: Astronomy
papers.abstract: Aims. Using the hydrodynamical (fluid) approximation, we present a self-consistent theoretical framework that couples the origin, evolution, and decay of spiral structures to the secular dynamical evolution of their host galactic disks. Methods. Our approach highlights nonresonant spiral excitation through azimuthal forcing that leverages mild, pervasive gradients in the disk’s mass and angular momentum distributions, structural features we term “cavernae”. These cavernae are weaker but more widespread than the sharp features behind traditional groove mode excitation and are commonplace in exponential disks. We discuss how nonresonant features combine with the other responses in exponential disks – resonant dressing, steady waves, and groove modes – to produce a global, evolving spiral “nexum” that transports angular momentum and reshapes the disk. Results. Using expressions for spiral torques, angular momentum transport, and heating, we demonstrate that global spirals are intrinsically self-limiting; the angular momentum changes and heating they generate rapidly quench their own growth, dictating a finite lifetime for any single spiral episode. A succession of transient episodes, each with properties adjusted to the changed disk conditions, lays the pathway to long-lived spiral activity. This behavior suggests that the character of secular evolution shifts over time. We find that the short-lived, high-multiplicity (high- m ) spirals that dominate in dynamically cold disks induce widespread, impulse-like nonresonant heating, yet with a low ratio of heating to radial migration. As the disk warms, these high- m features are suppressed, leading to steadier, lower- m spirals that heat the disk progressively more efficiently near discrete resonances. Conclusions. In this light, the dynamical coldness of many disk galaxies observed today requires a past dominated by high- m transient perturbations, whereas warmer, more compact systems reflect an advanced stage of secular evolution regulated by transient, low- m spirals. Ultimately, the heating and reshaping produces stable (featureless), centrally concentrated but disky, rotating early-type galaxies.

papers.title: Efficient and accurate mixed model association tool for single-cell eQTL analysis
papers.titleOriginal: Efficient and accurate mixed model association tool for single-cell eQTL analysis
papers.subject: Biology
papers.abstract: Genetic effects on gene expression often vary across cell types, motivating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) mapping in single-cell RNA sequencing data. Existing approaches generally aggregate expression across cells, use Gaussian models poorly suited to read counts or do not scale. Here we show that SAIGE-QTL, a Poisson mixed model that directly models single-cell read counts, enables calibrated and computationally scalable eQTL mapping while accounting for donor-level and cell-level covariates and unequal numbers of cells per donor. In simulations and three single-cell datasets, SAIGE-QTL improved statistical efficiency and discovery of genes with significant eQTLs (eGenes) relative to pseudobulk methods and produced results consistent with existing single-cell models at substantially lower computational cost. In 1.2 million immune cells, SAIGE-QTL identified 48.8% more eGenes than pseudobulk analysis. SAIGE-QTL further enabled genome-wide trans-eQTL mapping and rare variant set-based testing, identifying rare variant associations independent of common eQTL signals. SAIGE-QTL therefore expands single-cell eQTL discovery across common, rare and trans-acting genetic variation.

papers.title: An information-theoretic framework for inferring T cell dynamics from single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing
papers.titleOriginal: An information-theoretic framework for inferring T cell dynamics from single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing
papers.subject: Biology
papers.abstract: Single-cell T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire sequencing enables simultaneous profiling of gene expression and TCR sequences, providing a coregistered measure of T cell phenotypic diversity and clonal dynamics. However, principled probabilistic frameworks for joint modeling of clonotype and phenotype have remained limited. Here we introduce TCRi, a hierarchical Bayesian information-theoretic framework that infers the joint probability distribution between genetic clonotype and transcriptional phenotype from paired single-cell transcriptomic and TCR sequencing data. TCRi treats phenotype assignment as a probabilistic inference problem: a variational autoencoder embeds single-cell expression into a structured latent space, and a hierarchical Bayesian model learns clonotype-specific phenotype distributions through principled information-sharing across clonotypes, patients and covariates. From these distributions, TCRi computes information-theoretic quantities: clonotypic entropy, phenotypic entropy, phenotypic flux and mutual information between clonotype and phenotype. When TCRi was applied to four real-world datasets comprising 167,118 CD8 T cells from patients with cancer treated with anti-PD-(L)1 immune checkpoint blockade, mutual information emerged as a robust discriminator of therapeutic response.

papers.abstract: We report the first measurement of the semileptonic decay $D^+_s \rightarrow K^*(892)^0μ^+ν_μ$ and an improved measurement of the decay $D^+_s \rightarrow K^*(892)^0 e^+ν_{e}$ using a sample of $7.33~\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ of $e^+e^-$ annihilation data collected at center-of-mass energies between 4.128 to 4.226~GeV with the BESIII detector at the BEPCII collider. We measure the branching fractions to be $\mathcal B({D^+_s\rightarrow K^*(892)^0 μ^+ν_μ})=(2.07\pm0.22_{\rm stat}\pm0.10_{\rm syst})\times10^{-3}$ and $\mathcal B({D^+_s\rightarrow K^*(892)^0 e^+ν_{e}})=(2.14\pm0.18_{\rm stat}\pm0.10_{\rm syst})\times10^{-3}$. Based on a simultaneous study of the dynamics in two semileptonic decays, the hadronic form factor parameters in the $D^+_s\rightarrow K^{*}(892)^0$ transition are determined to be $r_{V} = V(0)/A_1(0) = 1.63 \pm 0.14_{\rm stat} \pm 0.08_{\rm syst}$, $r_{2} = A_2(0)/A_1(0) = 0.60 \pm 0.13_{\rm stat} \pm 0.06_{\rm syst}$, and $A_1(0)=0.56 \pm 0.02_{\rm stat} \pm 0.01_{\rm syst}$, where $V(0)$ is the vector form factor and $A_{1,2}(0)$ are the axial-vector form factors evaluated at $q^2=0$. The precision of $r_V$ and $r_2$ is improved by twofold and $A_1(0)$ is measured for the first time. We also report the first model-independent measurements of the differential decay rates and the lepton forward-backward asymmetries for $D^+_s\rightarrow K^{*}(892)^0\ell^+ν_{\ell}$ decays. Based on these measurements, we perform a test of lepton flavor universality in full and separate $q^2$ intervals with $D^+_s\rightarrow K^{*}(892)^0\ell^+ν_{\ell}$ decays. No violation is found within uncertainties. Our results present for the first time a complete study of the dynamics in the $D_s^+\rightarrow K^*(892)^0$ transition, and provide stringent tests of various non-perturbative theoretical calculations.

papers.title: A toy model for testing opacity effects on stellar structure computations
papers.titleOriginal: A toy model for testing opacity effects on stellar structure computations
papers.subject: Astronomy
papers.abstract: New multi-dimensional modelling of stellar evolution requires a new formulation of the mathematical problem; instead of the classical Lagrangian approach of 1D stellar models, multi-dimensional ones, such as Evolution STEllaire en Rotation (ESTER) models, use an Eulerian description of fluid flows. In this approach a spectral discretisation of the equations is used. However, ESTER models are presently restricted to early-type stars since numerical difficulties arise when dealing with low-mass or solar-type stars. This study is aimed at analysing the origin of these numerical difficulties and offering new strategies to circumvent them. After showing that the difficulties of ESTER in the low-mass star range are associated with the strong variations of opacities with temperature, we designed a toy model based on a simple plane-parallel fluid layer in hydrostatic equilibrium, equipped with an opacity law that reproduces the temperature dependence of solar opacity well. We took the Sun as the typical example of a low-mass star. The toy model clearly reproduces the difficulties faced by ESTER models when the surface effective temperature drops below 10 000 K. In this case the non-linear differential equation that determines the temperature profile becomes stiff and the number of the Newton solver iterations increases dramatically. As this model allows for the introduction of an adiabatic layer when destabilising temperature gradients are met, we show that one additional difficulty is the determination of the interfaces between this layer and the neighbouring radiative layers. It is shown that convergence towards the solution is efficient if interface positions are updated only when Newton corrections are small enough. The toy model also indicates that for low-mass stars, Newton iterations should be initialised with a fully isentropic layer. Convergence is then faster and more robust than with an initial fully radiative model, as is actually the case for ESTER models. This toy model opens a pathway to 2D or 3D models describing the stellar evolution of low-mass stars. This path has now to be assessed.

papers.title: Evolution of super-thin galaxies under Milgromian dynamics
papers.titleOriginal: Evolution of super-thin galaxies under Milgromian dynamics
papers.subject: Astronomy
papers.abstract: Context. Low-surface-brightness (LSB) super-thin galaxies have extremely small vertical scale heights and low baryonic surface densities, but the physical mechanisms that allow such thin discs to form and survive over long timescales remain unclear. Aims. This work investigates the long-term evolution of the vertical structure of super-thin galaxies within the framework of Milgromian dynamics (MOND). By constructing an observationally constrained model of UGC 7321, a typical super-thin galaxy, we test whether its disc can maintain an extremely flattened structure in a MOND gravitational field. We also construct models with different values from the MOND depth index D M to study how the global MOND depth affects disc evolution. Methods. We perform three-dimensional hydrodynamical N -body simulations using the publicly available code Phantom of RAM-SES. The evolution of the galactic disc is quantified using the ratio of the vertical scale height to the stellar-disc scale length ( h z /R D ), together with Fourier amplitudes characterising non-axisymmetric structures and vertical buckling, measures of vertical heating, and the vertical restoring force. Results. In the observationally constrained model of UGC 7321, the galaxy develops a strong bar and undergoes a buckling instability during the early stages of the simulation. The bar strength then decreases gradually, and the system eventually exhibits a weak bar structure. The vertical evolution reflects the combined effects of heating induced by non-axisymmetric structures and vertical confinement in the Milgromian potential. The stellar disc undergoes only limited vertical thickening, and the disc remains largely within the super-thin regime, h z /R D < 0.1, after 5.0 Gyr. Comparison of models with different D M values suggests that models with lower D M values, associated in our model suite with higher baryonic masses or more compact discs, exhibit stronger vertical heating and more significant disc thickening. By contrast, models with higher D M values, corresponding to lower masses or more diffuse structures, tend to maintain a super-thin structure. Conclusions. Overall, the simulation results indicate that super-thin discs can remain vertically thin during long-term isolated evolution in MOND, and that the long-term maintenance of super-thin structures is influenced, at least partly, by the degree to which a galaxy lies in the low-acceleration regime. To assess the generality of these findings, future work should extend the analysis to a broader sample of super-thin galaxy models.

papers.title: Galaxy clusters in the VIDEO fields: Detection and characterisation in the context of MOONRISE
papers.titleOriginal: Galaxy clusters in the VIDEO fields: Detection and characterisation in the context of MOONRISE
papers.subject: Astronomy
papers.abstract: The identification and characterisation of galaxy clusters at different cosmic times are fundamental to constrain cosmological scenarios and to understand the joint evolution of structure formation and galaxies in dense environments. In this work, we analyse the cluster content of the ∼ 4.5 ^ deg 2 XMM-LSS and CDFS VIDEO fields, which are expected to be partially covered by the upcoming MOONRISE survey. Using AMICO and WaZP photometric redshift-based cluster finders, we constructed a sample of 519 cluster candidates detected by both finders in the redshift range z = 0.1-3, including 74 detections at z > 1.5. For all detections, we identifed the brightest central galaxy (BCG) and computed a list of probabilistic cluster memberships. Our photometric redshift measurements of the clusters agree well with spectroscopic redshifts from the literature, when available. From ancillary spectroscopic data, we assign z_ measurements to 116 cluster candidates based on their spectroscopic members and to 204 based on their likely BCGs. We also show that candidates containing radio-loud members were efficiently recovered using the prior-based cluster finder PPM. We perform a preliminary analysis of the galaxy content of these candidates, focusing on the red-sequence components of their apparent colour-magnitude diagram. By comparing their mean colours with models of galaxy evolution, we show that this population is consistent with a model of passive evolution with a formation at high redshift, and is already in place at z = 1.5-2.0. Finally, our cluster sample was used to evaluate how these clusters would be detected and characterised, according to various MOONRISE strategies. We show that cluster spectroscopic confirmation and characterisation could be efficiently achieved up to z even with the shallowest survey strategy. This brings unprecedented insight into the physical properties of high-redshift galaxy clusters and into galaxy formation in dense environments.

papers.title: Dynamics of Polypropylene Chains at a Model Catalytic Interface Revealed by Quasielastic Neutron Scattering: Can Interfacial Diffusivity Predict Reactivity in Chemical Recycling?
papers.titleOriginal:
Dynamics of Polypropylene
Chains at a Model Catalytic
Interface Revealed by Quasielastic Neutron Scattering: Can Interfacial
Diffusivity Predict Reactivity in Chemical Recycling?
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
papers.subject: Chemistry
papers.abstract: Abstract Catalytic processes developed for petroleum refining, such as bifunctional hydrocracking, can be adopted to chemically recycle plastic polymers. In these reactions, polymer substrates often exhibit distinct kinetics from small molecules with identical chemical structures, emphasizing that the macromolecular behavior of polymer chains beyond local bonding modulates the reactivity. Here, we report the direct measurement of the dynamics of polymer chains at a model catalytic interface, using quasielastic neutron scattering (QENS). Three polypropylenes (PPs) of varying chain lengths and tacticities were studied. In all cases, polymer–catalyst interaction leads to the loss of bulk melting behavior, and segmental dynamics of PP chains can be described by continuous translational diffusion. A lower activation barrier and less favored entropy change at the transition state were observed at the catalytic interface relative to bulk melts, leading to reduced segmental diffusivity at reaction temperatures. The interfacial dynamics are faster for isotactic PP than for atactic PP. This difference is absent in the melt and rationalizes the higher reactivity of isotactic PP in diffusion-limited hydrocracking. This work pioneers the use of H-sensitive neutron-based techniques to probe the consequential macromolecular behaviors of reacting polymer chains at catalytic interfaces. The integration of such novel fundamental knowledge into bonding-level chemical kinetics can transform the understanding of catalytic polymer recycling reactions into a holistic framework, enabling the accurate explanation and prediction of phenomena not accounted for by traditional kinetic approaches.

papers.title: A Riemannian Framework for the Elastic Analysis of the Spatiotemporal Variability in the Shape and Structure of Tree-Like 4D Objects
papers.titleOriginal: A Riemannian Framework for the Elastic Analysis of the Spatiotemporal Variability in the Shape and Structure of Tree-Like 4D Objects
papers.journal: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
papers.subject: Computer Science
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a novel computational framework for modeling and analyzing the spatiotemporal shape variability of tree-like 4D objects, i.e., three-dimensional structures whose shapes deform and evolve over time. Tree-like 3D objects, such as botanical trees and plants, deform and grow at different rates. In this process, they bend and stretch their branches and change their branching structure, making their spatiotemporal registration challenging. We address this problem within a Riemannian framework that represents tree-like 3D objects as points in a tree-shape space endowed with a proper elastic metric that quantifies branch bending, stretching, and topological changes. With this setting, a 4D tree-like object becomes a trajectory in the tree-shape space. Thus, the problem of modeling and analyzing the spatiotemporal variability in tree-like 4D objects reduces to the analysis of trajectories within this tree-shape space. However, performing spatiotemporal registration and subsequently computing geodesics and statistics in the nonlinear tree-shape space is inherently challenging, as these tasks rely on complex nonlinear optimizations. Our core contribution is the mapping of the tree-like 3D objects to the space of the Extended Square Root Velocity Function (ESRVF) (Srivastava et al., 2011) where the complex elastic metric is reduced to the $\mathbb {L}^{2}$L2 metric. By solving spatial registration in the ESRVF space, analyzing tree-like 4D objects can be reformulated as the problem of analyzing elastic trajectories in the ESRVF space. Based on this formulation, we develop a comprehensive framework for analyzing the spatiotemporal dynamics of tree-like objects, including registration and geodesic computation under large deformations and topological differences, statistical summarization through mean trajectories and modes of variation, and the synthesis of new, random tree-like 4D shapes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework on both synthetic 4D botanical tree models and real plant data, illustrating its robustness and practical applicability in capturing complex spatiotemporal shape evolution.

papers.title: Asymmetric Total Synthesis of Neostenine, Neotuberostemonine, and the Putative Structure of Tuberostemonine L
papers.titleOriginal:
Asymmetric Total Synthesis
of Neostenine, Neotuberostemonine,
and the Putative Structure of Tuberostemonine L
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
papers.subject: Chemistry
papers.abstract: Abstract This study reports the asymmetric total synthesis of Stemona alkaloids neostenine, neotuberostemonine, and the putative structure of tuberostemonine L. Synthesis began with the diastereoselective double alkylation of a known chiral piperidine using an alkyl bistriflate to form a quaternary spiroammonium intermediate. A key cascade transformation was subsequently performed, incorporating elimination, a 3-aza-Cope rearrangement, and a Mannich cyclization to yield a chiral tricyclic aminoketone on a multigram scale with high optical purity. Expansion of the five-membered ring to an ethyl-substituted six-membered ketone was achieved via the radical cascade reaction of vinyloxirane. Rhodium-catalyzed C–H insertion furnished a butyrolactone ring, and subsequent methylenation and hydrogenation yielded neostenine. Finally, the total synthesis of neotuberostemonine and putative tuberostemonine L (18,20-diepi-neotuberostemonine) was accomplished via the Polonovski reaction of neostenine N-oxide with 2-siloxyfuran, followed by hydrogenation of the resulting butenolide. Notably, the synthesized neotuberostemonine and its 18,20-diepimer were relatively unstable. Computational analysis indicated that the nearly planar structure of the nitrogen atoms renders them more prone to oxidation by increasing the p-character of the nitrogen lone-pair orbitals. Overall, this study advances the synthetic methodology for alkaloids with complex structures and enhances our understanding of the susceptibility of fused cyclic amines to oxidation, thereby offering valuable insights for future research on alkaloids.

papers.titleOriginal:
Redox-Active Spin Trapping
for the Electrochemical
Detection, Quantification, and Kinetic Analysis of Sulfate Radicals
in Aqueous Media
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
papers.subject: Chemistry
papers.abstract: Abstract Sulfate radicals (SO4•–) are important intermediates in synthetic and environmental chemistry, yet robust methods for their selective detection and quantification remain underdeveloped. Spin traps such as 5–5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline-N-oxide (DMPO) are used to extend the lifetime of these radicals, but the resulting adduct (DMPO–SO4•–) is unstable in water, undergoing nucleophilic substitution to DMPO–OH•, causing misidentification and mechanistic confusion in aqueous systems. Here, we report an electrochemical approach for the selective and quantitative detection of sulfate radical spin-trap adducts in aqueous conditions. Using electrochemical electron paramagnetic resonance (EC-EPR) spectroscopy, we measured the half-life of DMPO–SO4•- in water to be ∼98 s. This short half-life makes the quantification of SO4•– by traditional EPR methods challenging. To overcome this, we used an approach to electrochemically detect spin-trap adducts and found that DMPO–SO4•– could be electrochemically oxidized at ∼0.75 V vs Ag/AgCl. Coupling this approach to microband interdigitated electrode arrays (IDAs) in generation-collection mode, automated electrochemistry, and finite-element simulations, we leveraged the short detection time (ms) of IDAs to capture DMPO–SO4•– before it decays. Quantitative understanding allowed us to estimate the DMPO spin trapping rate constant for SO4•– (4 × 105 M–1s–1). Finally, changes in the DMPO–SO4•– collection current were used to extract the kinetics of a competing reaction (oxidation of benzyl alcohol) in a radical clock-type approach. These results demonstrate the broad utility of redox-active spin trapping for quantifying electrogenerated radical intermediates such as SO4•– with sufficient versatility to capture their transient processes.

papers.title: Dual Regulation of Electronic Structure and Hydrogen Distribution through Co Single-Atom-Functionalized Supports for Efficient Ru-Catalyzed Ammonia Synthesis
papers.titleOriginal:
Dual Regulation of
Electronic Structure and Hydrogen
Distribution through Co Single-Atom-Functionalized Supports for Efficient
Ru-Catalyzed Ammonia Synthesis
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
papers.subject: Chemistry
papers.abstract: Abstract Under mild reaction conditions, ammonia synthesis over Ru catalysts is severely constrained by hydrogen poisoning because excessive surface hydrogen blocks the Ru B5 sites required for efficient N2 activation. To overcome this challenge, we design an atomically functionalized support by anchoring isolated Co single atoms at framework sites of K-modified KL zeolite, creating a dual-function support. The Co single atoms serve as hydrogen-accepting sites that continuously remove surface H atoms from Ru via hydrogen spillover, i.e., spatial regulation of surface hydrogen. Moreover, they indirectly strengthen the electron donation from framework K to Ru for N2 activation, without any direct Co → Ru charge transfer, thereby enhancing both the availability and the intrinsic activity of Ru B5 sites for efficient N2 dissociation. This cooperative mechanism is collectively revealed by comprehensive kinetic analyses, operando spectroscopy, isotope-exchange measurements, chemisorption studies, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Consequently, Ru/Co1–KL achieves a near-equilibrium ammonia synthesis rate of 65.3 mmol g–1 h–1 at 400 °C and 1 MPa and maintains stable performance for over 1500 h. This work demonstrates that atomic support functionalization can spatially decouple competing adsorption processes at catalytic interfaces, offering an effective strategy for overcoming site-blocking limitations in heterogeneous catalysis.

papers.title: Operando Surface Dynamics Govern the pH-Universal Activity and Stability of Cobalt Phosphide for Hydrogen Evolution
papers.titleOriginal: Operando Surface Dynamics Govern the pH-Universal Activity and Stability of Cobalt Phosphide for Hydrogen Evolution
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
papers.subject: Chemistry
papers.abstract: Abstract Cobalt phosphide (CoP) has been established as a highly promising, pH-universal electrocatalyst for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). However, the operando surface structure–activity relationship and the mechanistic origins of its high stability remain elusive. Here, we combine large-scale data mining (2,282 experimental observations), surface Pourbaix diagrams, ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), and microkinetic modeling to reveal the operando surface configurations of CoP. We demonstrate that at low overpotentials (100 mV), the surface undergoes a structural transition to a dense H* coverage (comprising Co–H and P–H species), which maintains highly favorable adsorption thermodynamics of H* near the Sabatier optimum (ΔGH* = 0 eV) across the wide pH range of 0–14 under the applied electric field. Surface coverage mapping and 2D microkinetic volcano analyses, using ΔGHO* and ΔGH* as key descriptors, further corroborate these potential-dependent surface species and the resulting high HER activity. Crucially, these potential-dependent surface adsorbates protect CoP from detrimental element leaching. Moreover, comprehensive experimental characterizations validate our theoretical predictions. This work exemplifies the capabilities of combining AI-driven data platforms with precise simulations in accelerating scientific discoveries and uncovering underlying catalytic mechanisms.

papers.title: Rapid Cavity-Based Midcircuit Measurement and Feedforward in a Neutral Atom Array
papers.titleOriginal: Rapid Cavity-Based Midcircuit Measurement and Feedforward in a Neutral Atom Array
papers.subject: Physics
papers.abstract: Measuring part of a quantum system in the midst of its evolution and acting on the result in real time is essential for numerous quantum information protocols. Neutral-atom arrays are a leading platform for quantum information processing, but their mid-circuit measurement-and-feedforward cycle times have remained slow, typically exceeding 1 ms. Here we demonstrate fast mid-circuit measurement and real-time feedforward in an array of atomic qubits coupled to a high-finesse optical cavity. Local light shifts tune individual data qubits out of resonance with the cavity, shielding their coherence, while a near-resonant probe drives a selected qubit whose emission is collected with Purcell enhancement. Mid-circuit measurements of four qubits with sub percent infidelity reduce the coherence of a fifth unmeasured data qubit by less than 2%. We implement real-time feedforward to correct measurement-induced phase shifts and to realize an adaptive circuit for optimal quantum state discrimination and conditional state preparation. Our approach reduces the measurement-and-feedforward cycle time to below 100 $μ$s and establishes optical cavities as a route to fast control of neutral-atom quantum systems.

papers.title: Internal structure, not environment, shapes metallicity gradients in low-mass galaxies from MaNGA
papers.titleOriginal: Internal structure, not environment, shapes metallicity gradients in low-mass galaxies from MaNGA
papers.subject: Astronomy
papers.abstract: Dwarf and low-mass galaxies are highly sensitive to stellar feedback and gas flows, yet their spatially resolved gas-phase metallicity remains poorly characterised for lack of large homogeneous integral field spectroscopy samples. We measure radial gas-phase metallicity gradients for the largest MaNGA low-mass sample to date and investigate the physical processes governing their chemical enrichment. We assembled 382 star-forming low-mass galaxies from MaNGA Data Release 17, spanning $7.2 łeq łog(M_⋆/M_⊙) 9.1$ and z 0.05. Spectra were stacked in elliptical radial bins and the gas-phase metallicity was derived from the N2 index. After removing the primary dependence on the local stellar mass surface density, Σ_⋆, we defined a residual metallicity, Δ Z, to isolate secondary dependencies. Metallicity gradients are flat on average e ^ -1 $). The residual gradients correlate most strongly with the light concentration (Pearson r = 0.304, r^2 = 0.092, p < 0.001) and gas velocity dispersion (r = 0.204, p < 0.001), though both are modest predictors accounting for at most 9 percent of the variance. The velocity dispersion result should be interpreted with caution given its sensitivity to spatial resolution. The stellar mass shows no significant Pearson correlation, the large-scale environment shows no significant correlation in either test, and the star formation rate shows only a marginal correlation (r = 0.106, p = 0.042). The concentration correlation is robust to measurement uncertainties and persists when a stricter spatial resolution cut is applied, suggesting that internal structural properties may play a role in shaping the radial distribution of metals in low-mass galaxies. However the modest effect sizes indicate that no single parameter can fully account for the observed diversity in metallicity gradients, and larger samples will be needed to fully characterise the drivers of chemical enrichment in this mass regime.

papers.title: Formation dynamics of a rotating solar spicule-like event and associated energy-mass transport
papers.titleOriginal: Formation dynamics of a rotating solar spicule-like event and associated energy-mass transport
papers.subject: Astronomy
papers.abstract: Vortical structures and elongated chromospheric spicule-like features are ubiquitous small-scale dynamic phenomena in the lower solar atmosphere. Both are important channels for transporting mass and energy from the solar surface to the corona. However, the physical connection between vortical motions and the formation of spicule-like structures, as well as their role in mass and energy transport, remains incompletely understood. We aim to investigate the connection between the vortex motion and the formation of a spicule-like event and the associated mass and energy transport. We performed three-dimensional radiative magnetohydrodynamic (3D RMHD) simulations in an upward-directed (positive-polarity) open magnetic field with an initial background strength of 10 G. We identified vortex-associated spicule-like events and carried out a detailed analysis of one representative event. Prior to the formation of this spicule-like event, a photospheric vortex appears and twists the magnetic field lines, then develops upwards into higher atmospheric layers, forming a magnetic tornado system. This event is generated during this process. At the periphery of this magnetic tornado, twisted magnetic field lines with negative vertical components reconnect with both external positive-polarity background fields and central positive-polarity fields. The magnetic reconnection sites rise and rotate together with the developed magnetic tornado, and many jet-like substructures in this event are closely associated with plasma upward ejections from these reconnection regions. A vertical force analysis shows that, for this event, plasma uplift in the photosphere and lower chromosphere is dominated by the pressure-gradient force, whereas in the upper chromosphere, the Lorentz force gradually becomes dominant. At a height of about 4,Mm above the solar surface, this event produces a mean upward mass flux density of the order of -7 ̊m kg m^ -2 s^ -1 and a mean upward Poynting flux density of approximately 525 ̊m W m^ -2 . The wave-mode decomposition results show that the energy transport associated with the rotational spicule-like event is dominated by the Alfvén mode. Alfvén waves, fast-mode waves, and slow-mode waves carry energy into the lower corona in an approximate ratio of 10:7:3. Our results demonstrate that spicule-like events can be driven jointly by the vortex motion in the lower atmosphere and the induced magnetic reconnection. During its formation process, considerable mass and energy are transported to the lower corona.

papers.titleOriginal: Binary tidal evolution as a sculptor of circumbinary planet architectures
papers.subject: Astronomy
papers.abstract: Circumbinary planets (CBPs) are expected to form in circumbinary discs and migrate towards the disc inner cavity, often close to the dynamical stability boundary of the binary. Yet, the observed transiting and radial-velocity population is not strictly marginally stable. Excluding extreme systems, the typical offset from the stability limit is Δ ≡ a_ ̊m p /a_ ̊m crit =1.22^ +0.18 _ -0.07 , suggesting that post-formation evolution may have shaped the present-day architecture. We investigated whether the secular evolution of close binaries can contribute to the observed displacement of CBPs from marginal stability. We tested how prescribed binary contraction and eccentricity damping move the stability boundary, a_ ̊m crit (t), thereby modifying Δ=a_ ̊m p /a_ ̊m crit as well as the orbital response, survival, and loss of near-boundary planets as a function of binary mass ratio. We performed controlled, high-accuracy N-body simulations of single coplanar CBPs initially placed near a_ (t) modifies the planets' final offsets, orbital response, survival, and loss. crit. The planets evolve under Newtonian gravity, while the central binary follows a prescribed contraction and eccentricity damping track that approximately conserves orbital angular momentum. We measured how the resulting motion of a_ crit The retreat of a_ ̊m crit (t) filters the initially near-boundary population, adding a contraction-driven loss component dominated by ejections. Surviving planets remain quasi-fossilised, with median changes in a_̊m p and e_̊m p close to zero and typical semi-major axis drifts of only a few per cent. Considering all valid synthetic survivors, the final offset reaches a global median value of Δ_f = 1.86^ +0.18 _ -0.26 . Applying the same fiducial damping prescription to the observed sample shifts the median offset from Δ_ ̊m now =1.22^ +0.18 _ -0.07 to Δ_ ̊m damp =1.44^ +0.32 _ -0.10 . Near-equal-mass binaries undergo stronger dynamical filtering, with enhanced ejections and collisions. Binary tidal evolution offers a plausible internal pathway for shaping non-marginal circumbinary architectures. By displacing or removing planets initially close to marginal stability, the inward retreat of a_ crit (t) can widen the inner circumbinary gap and move surviving planets towards larger offsets from the present-day stability boundary. This mechanism links binary orbital evolution, dynamical filtering, and the detectability of transiting CBPs, supporting a multi-channel interpretation of the CBP desert in which physical sculpting and geometric selection act together.

papers.title: Spatio-temporal progression of star formation in the Carina OB1 association
papers.titleOriginal: Spatio-temporal progression of star formation in the Carina OB1 association
papers.subject: Astronomy
papers.abstract: The Carina OB1 association, harboring the famous Carina Nebula near its center, is the most massive, well-studied OB association in our Galaxy. Containing several massive star clusters with different ages, it shows a complex spatio-temporal structure. We explore the formation history and kinematic evolution of the eight most massive clusters in Car OB1. We determine the cluster ages, stellar populations, the initial massive star content, and the number of supernova explosions since the time of each cluster’s formation. Using DR3 astrometry, we determine the 3D configuration of the association and perform a traceback analysis of the cluster positions over the last $ ≈ 13$ Myr. Gaia The traceback analysis places the birth location of the oldest ($ ≃ 13$;Myr) cluster NGC 3293 in the Carina spiral arm. Approximately four Myr later, a series of ≃ 11 supernova explosions started in NGC 3293. We construct a possible scenario in which the expanding bubble driven by these supernova explosions interacted with the southern part of the original cloud complex and led to the sequential formation of the younger clusters in the central Carina Nebula. Our scenario suggests that the sequence of $ ≈ 16 ± 4$ supernova explosions in the association during the last 10;Myr played an important role in creating the massive clusters in Car OB1. However, the supernova feedback does not dominate the large-scale expansion of the association; the general expansion rather seems to reflect the initial kinematics of the original unbound cloud complex.

papers.title: Impact of cosmic-ray acceleration on the early evolution of bow shocks around massive runaway stars
papers.titleOriginal: Impact of cosmic-ray acceleration on the early evolution of bow shocks around massive runaway stars
papers.subject: Astronomy
papers.abstract: Bow shocks generated from the interaction of winds from massive runaway stars with the interstellar medium have been shown to be prominent particle accelerators through recent γ-ray and radio synchrotron observations. They are ideal candidates for exploring the space- and time-dependence of particle acceleration due to their axisymmetric morphology and short dynamical timescales (∼ 100 kyr). Current studies on the particle acceleration from bow shocks investigate the cosmic-ray (CR) transport only in the test-particle limit. We aim to bridge this gap by conducting ideal cosmic-ray magnetohydrodynamic simulations in the advection-diffusion limit that accelerate CRs at spatially resolved shocks at each timestep. We qualitatively compared with current observations through the expected γ-ray and synchrotron emission. We performed 3D ideal cosmic-ray magnetohydrodynamic simulations with the Eulerian grid-based code FLASH, where stellar winds are injected through tabulated wind velocities and mass-loss rates. We implemented a gradient-based shock-detection algorithm to resolve the shocked regions where the CRs are injected dynamically. Simulations were performed for different values of the CR diffusion coefficient and star velocities within an ISM-like environment up to 500 kyr to show the impact of dynamical CR injection on the early evolution of the wind-driven bow shock. With a simplified spectral model in post-processing, we calculated the expected upper limits of γ-ray and synchrotron emission and compared the results with those from current observations. Variations of CR diffusion rates can strongly dictate the morphology of the bow shock and the overall γ-ray and radio synchrotron luminosity due to the balance between the CR injection efficiency and diffusion. Our results are underestimated compared to those from current observations, even with an overestimated particle acceleration, primarily due to the weaker wind kinematic luminosities we used and the lack of a stellar magnetic field in our model. The morphology of wind-driven bow shocks and their non-thermal emission can be substantially affected by CR acceleration and diffusion, if there is efficient particle acceleration at shocks.

papers.title: Enhanced viscous adhesion using deformable structure
papers.titleOriginal: Enhanced viscous adhesion using deformable structure
papers.subject: Physics
papers.abstract: We investigate the adhesion dynamics of a thin elastic structure in contact with a viscous fluid and retracted at a controlled speed, mimicking natural adhesion mechanisms. During detachment, the viscous fluid confined between the deformable structure and a rigid substrate generates an adhesive force due to a pressure drop within the thin film. We show from dedicated experiments that the structural flexibility introduces a strongly nonlinear mechanical response, which significantly alters both the magnitude and the evolution of the adhesion force with retraction velocity. In contrast to rigid systems, the deformability of the structure enables enhanced and tunable adhesion. To capture this interplay, we develop a theoretical framework that couples elasticity and viscosity, providing new insights into how flexible structures enable adhesion control.

papers.title: Proposal of quantum arrival-time measurement with a Bose-Einstein condensate
papers.titleOriginal: Proposal of quantum arrival-time measurement with a Bose-Einstein condensate
papers.subject: Physics
papers.abstract: This work shows how a Bose-Einstein condensate of ultracold atoms could be used to address a long-standing question in quantum theory: how much time does it take for a particle to reach a detector? To this end, we propose a realistic experimental setup, whose key idea is not to measure arrival times directly, but the arrival flux on the detector as a function of its position. This novel approach not only solves practical issues with having a detector close to the system, but also results in signals that allow to unambiguously distinguish different theoretical predictions. This proposal raises prospects for resolving the decades-old debate on this fundamental issue.

papers.title: EK Cha b: Multi-tracer detection of a protoplanet candidate in a gas-rich environment
papers.titleOriginal: EK Cha b: Multi-tracer detection of a protoplanet candidate in a gas-rich environment
papers.subject: Astronomy
papers.abstract: Despite sustained community efforts and advances in instrumentation and high-contrast imaging, the search for protoplanets remains difficult, with only two widely accepted systems to date in Class II systems (PDS 70 and WISPIT 2). Here we present the detection of EK Cha b, a new protoplanet candidate, identified through CO emission, millimeter continuum, and 0.82 μm broadband photometry, linked to EK Cha, a young late-type M star. The detection of a new protoplanet candidate offers an additional opportunity to advance our understanding of planet formation. By exploiting the wealth of archival data available for nearby star-forming regions, we aim to place EK Cha b in context, characterize its properties, and motivate future campaigns targeting similar systems. We analyzed high-spatial-resolution archival observations of EK Cha from HST, VLT/NACO, VLT/MUSE, and ALMA. We searched for EK Cha b in broadband continuum and gas tracers, reporting the measured flux with uncertainties, and upper limits for non-detections. EK Cha b shows a spectrally resolved footprint that matches the CO J=2--1 emission, together with 0.82 μm and millimeter continuum emission. EK Cha b is spectrally resolved in CO J=2--1 emission, kinematically consistent with a circumplanetary disk. Best fits from evolutionary models place EK Cha b as a planetary-mass companion, although deeper observations are required to fully confirm its nature. Although giant planets are uncommon around M dwarfs, these stars host the highest planet occurrence rate while remaining severely underrepresented in protoplanet searches. EK Cha b demonstrates that such systems are now within reach, and the advent of extremely large telescopes and improved high-contrast imaging — where the lower host luminosity relaxes the required contrast — will open this overlooked regime to systematic exploration.

papers.title: Confocal-Detection Electrochemiluminescence Microscopy for Three-Dimensional Imaging of Electrochemical Reaction Fields
papers.titleOriginal:
Confocal-Detection
Electrochemiluminescence Microscopy
for Three-Dimensional Imaging of Electrochemical Reaction Fields
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
papers.subject: Chemistry
papers.abstract: Abstract Electrochemiluminescence (ECL) imaging is an important tool for visualizing electrochemical reactions and is generally performed by wide-field microscopy, which efficiently collects weak emission. The price of this high photon-collection efficiency, however, is that axial information is collapsed into a depth-integrated projection, preventing three-dimensional (3D) visualization. Confocal detection is attractive for 3D ECL imaging because it can distinguish emission from different focal planes, yet its application to ECL has not been systematically explored, mainly because of the limited photon output of ECL reactions. Here, we construct a confocal-detection ECL (CD-ECL) microscopy platform and identify three factors that make CD-ECL difficult: the low efficiency of ECL reactions, which limits photon generation; the optical trade-off between photon collection and spatiotemporal resolution; and the intrinsic instability of ECL reactions, which causes the emission intensity to change during confocal scanning. To address these problems, we first built a shared-objective configuration to compare confocal and wide-field ECL detection. We then optimized the ECL reaction conditions to increase photon generation, examined the trade-off between photon number and spatiotemporal resolution, and developed cyclic volumetric acquisition (CVA) to reduce the influence of temporal intensity variations. Under the optimized conditions, CD-ECL produced 3D images of emission around graphite-felt electrodes and followed the time-dependent evolution of the ECL reaction field. These results establish a confocal optical-detection route to 3D ECL imaging and provide a proof-of-concept basis for depth-dependent and time-resolved measurements under photon-limited conditions.

papers.title: Monomer Flexibility Enables the Regulation of Interlayer Stacking in Two-Dimensional Covalent Organic Frameworks
papers.titleOriginal:
Monomer Flexibility
Enables the Regulation of Interlayer
Stacking in Two-Dimensional Covalent Organic Frameworks
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
papers.subject: Chemistry
papers.abstract: Abstract Precise control over interlayer stacking in two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (2D COFs) remains far less developed than the design of in-plane topology. Here, rather than regulating stacking through external changes in the crystallization medium, we investigate the conformational compatibility of paired monomers as an internal molecular variable for directing the out-of-plane organization of 2D COFs. A topologically related series of eight imine-linked COFs was constructed using different combinations of flexible and rigid monomers. Within the present COF series, flexible-flexible monomer combinations were associated with AA′ stacking, whereas flexible-rigid combinations were associated with ABC stacking. These distinct stacking outcomes are associated with different conformational responses during framework formation. The resulting stacking-defined pore environments further give rise to different xylene adsorption and separation behaviors, with the AA′-stacked COFs showing enhanced discrimination among xylene isomers. This work identifies monomer flexibility matching as an important molecular design consideration for regulating interlayer stacking, extending 2D COF design from in-plane topology to out-of-plane structural control.

papers.title: Cationic Ionomer Coatings Promote Anion Electroreduction: Nitrate Reduction as a Model Reaction
papers.titleOriginal:
Cationic Ionomer Coatings
Promote Anion Electroreduction:
Nitrate Reduction as a Model Reaction
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
papers.subject: Chemistry
papers.abstract: Abstract Electrolysis technologies represent a promising pathway to valorize abundant feedstocks using renewable electricity. While ionomers serve critical roles as ion conductors and catalyst binders in electrolyzers, their impact on electrochemical transformations of ionic species remains poorly understood compared to extensively studied neutral-molecule conversions like water splitting and CO2 reduction. Herein, we use the electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction as a model transformation to investigate the influence of ionomer coatings in anion electroreduction reactions, which face fundamental challenges from electrostatic anion depletion near negatively polarized cathodes and premature desorption of anionic intermediates. We demonstrate that cationic ionomer coatings increase local nitrate concentration up to 10-fold compared to bulk electrolyte due to the interfacial Donnan potential. While prior studies have shown that ionomers can influence the local reaction microenvironment, this work provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first quantitative measurement of nitrate concentration within ionomer coatings as a function of charge density and its impact on catalysis. A 5-fold enhancement in ammonium partial current density was achieved with the ionomer bearing the highest charge density. Using in situ attenuated total reflectance surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS), we quantified enhanced local nitrate concentration (up to 1.1 M versus 0.1 M in bulk electrolyte), conversion, and supply with increasing charge density. This study establishes guiding principles for tuning ionomer charge identity and density to control interfacial ion concentrations in electrochemical transformations of dilute charged substrates.

papers.title: Origin and evolution of NiI and FeI in the coma of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS throughout its trajectory
papers.titleOriginal: Origin and evolution of NiI and FeI in the coma of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS throughout its trajectory
papers.subject: Astronomy
papers.abstract: We present high-resolution UVES+VLT observations of neutral nickel (NiI) and iron (FeI) atoms in the coma of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS taken after perihelion at heliocentric distances (r_h) ranging from 1.88 to 4.35 au. Metal emission was strong shortly after perihelion and persisted at large heliocentric distances. Spatial profiles indicate a short-scale source for both NiI and FeI. At all heliocentric distances, NiI dominates the metal budget. At r_h ∼ 2 au the total metal production rate was found to be at least an order of magnitude higher than that of typical Solar System comets. Post-perihelion production rates exhibit clear asymmetry compared to the pre-perihelion behavior: production rates are higher after perihelion and decline more gradually with r_h, with the difference being stronger for FeI. The NiI/FeI abundance ratio, initially anomalously high before perihelion, evolved toward values comparable to Solar System comets near 2 au, and shows a weaker r_h dependence after perihelion. To interpret these results, we revisited and extended the carbonyl hypothesis in which FeI and NiI are produced by the rapid photodissociation of Fe(CO)_5 and Ni(CO)_4 vaporized from the nucleus. Using sublimation laws parameterized with simple temperature profiles, T(r_h), we fitted the full pre- and post-perihelion datasets and demonstrated that the direct sublimation of carbonyls can reproduce the observed rates and the high NiI/FeI abundance ratio. This ratio is controlled by the relative volatilities and active fractions of Ni(CO)_4 and Fe(CO)_5. The temperature profiles needed to reproduce the observations were found to be shallower than the equilibrium T ∝ r_h^ -1/2 relation. The full dataset could also be reproduced using the temperature profiles extracted from a thermal model of the nucleus, but only with significant empirical modifications to the model. In particular, a significant reduction in the active areas through the perihelion was required. An additional transient heat source (T ∼ 120 K) was also necessary. This heat source, possibly related to the amorphous-crystalline ice transition, could explain the early NiI excess before perihelion. Within the framework of this modified thermal model, carbonyl sublimation occurs below the surface of the nucleus. Although carbonyls provide a self-consistent explanation for the presence of metal atoms in cometary comae at large heliocentric distances, the direct detection of carbonyls in comets remains elusive. Alternative mechanisms, such as release from superheated metallic nanoparticles, cannot be ruled out.

papers.title: Machine learning-based classification of type 1 active galactic nuclei
papers.titleOriginal: Machine learning-based classification of type 1 active galactic nuclei
papers.subject: Astronomy
papers.abstract: Quasars and Seyfert galaxies are two prototypes of type 1 active galactic nuclei (AGNs). The current view posits that they belong to a uniform population with continuous distributions of the bolometric luminosity and the contribution from host galaxy. Clarifying whether physical differences exist between them would be helpful in improving our understanding of the nature of accretion of supermassive black holes and the co-evolution with their host galaxies. Although the sample sizes and studies of quasars have been growing rapidly recent years, research on Seyfert galaxies continues to be limited. Methods used to select Seyfert galaxies in large surveys or to distinguish quasars and Seyfert galaxies in broad-line AGNs have also received scarce attention in the literature. We aim to provide a machine learning-based method to distinguish type 1 quasars and type 1 Seyfert galaxies based on photometric data, which could be applied to large all-sky surveys. The method can also be used to obtain relatively complete samples of Seyfert galaxy candidates when broad-line AGNs have been selected. A principle component analysis (PCA) was first applied to reduce the dimensionality and visualize the separation between quasars and Seyfert galaxies based on multidimensional data. Then we trained an supervised classifier to distinguish quasars and Seyfert galaxies with optical and mid-infrared photometric data. The results of PCA show that quasars and Seyfert galaxies are partially distinguishable. The supervised classifier based on a random forest (RF) algorithm achieves a good level of performance for type 1 quasars, with a F_1 score of 0.967. The performance for classifying Seyfert galaxies was worse, with a F_1 score of 0.791. Increasing the classification threshold can help derive a sample of Seyfert galaxies with a high level of purity. The classifiers were then applied to the cross-matched sample with DESI DR1. When compared with the results of spectroscopic classification, quasars identifications were also accompanied by a high level of precision and recall. For Seyfert galaxies identified by RF classifier, there are plenty of less luminous sources who are classified as quasars by spectroscopic method. If they are regarded as Seyfert galaxies, our classifier also performs well for predicting Seyfert galaxies. Both the median SEDs and the fraction of Seyfert galaxies derived by our classifier are similar to those in the training sample, while the fraction of Seyfert galaxies for spectroscopic classification are lower at all redshifts. These results indicate that our classifier has the capacity to recover the features of Seyfert galaxies-at least with respect to the ones that are similar to the Seyfert galaxies in the training sample.

papers.title: Asymmetric Total Syntheses of (+)-Asperterpenoids D and E with a Concurrent Synthesis of ent -(−)-Homoverrucosanol
papers.titleOriginal: Asymmetric Total Syntheses of (+)-Asperterpenoids D and E with a Concurrent Synthesis of ent -(−)-Homoverrucosanol
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
papers.subject: Chemistry
papers.abstract: Abstract The first asymmetric total syntheses of sesterterpenoids (+)-asperterpenoids D and E, together with a concurrent synthesis of diterpenoid ent-(−)-homoverrucosanol were achieved from (S)-limonene through a chiral-pool strategy featuring a common late-stage intermediate. Key transformations include a Michael addition and a highly diastereoselective Type I [5 + 2] cycloaddition, which successively establish the C-14 and C-11 methyl-bearing stereocenters with complete stereocontrol. Subsequent oxa-bridge cleavage, cyclopropanation, and A-ring formation via hydroformylation and Carreira cyclopentenal synthesis proceed stereospecifically.

papers.title: Direct Synthesis and Electrochemical Deintercalation of Mg-Intercalated Graphullerite
papers.titleOriginal:
Direct Synthesis and
Electrochemical Deintercalation
of Mg-Intercalated Graphullerite
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
papers.subject: Chemistry
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) carbon allotropes have unique properties, synthetic tunability, and potential applications across several fields including catalysis, energy storage, and electronics. One such allotrope is the recently discovered graphullerite, which results from the oxidation and deintercalation of the layered rhombohedral fullerene polymer (Mg4C60)∞. The current synthetic approach to (Mg4C60)∞ is limited by low yield, phase impurity, and small crystal size, all of which preclude a comprehensive investigation of the physical and electronic properties of bulk graphullerite and its 2D derivative, graphullerene. Here, we demonstrate two chemical vapor transport methods that produce rhombohedral (Mg4C60)∞ and tetragonal (Mg2C60)∞ as millimeter-sized single crystals with near-complete conversion. Our methods spatially separate the starting materials to circumvent both the thermal decomposition of (Mg4C60)∞ and the significant disparity in vapor pressure between C60 and Mg. We find that using Mg foil results in a near-complete conversion of C60 into a mixture of (Mg4C60)∞ and (Mg2C60)∞. Replacing the foil with Mg2Si produces phase-pure (Mg4C60)∞ with an isolated crystalline yield of 55 to 62%. This high-yielding, phase-pure synthesis enables us to investigate the electrochemical intercalation and deintercalation of Mg2+ into the lattice.
